reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Reshaping Data in Postgres
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 10, Reshaping Data in Postgres.

Before we begin, think about what you have already learned in this course. You learned how relational tables are organized. You learned how to filter rows, group data, join tables, use subqueries, and work with text and dates. In Module 9, you focused on cleaning data. You profiled messy values, standardized them carefully, checked quality rules, and preserved uncertainty instead of guessing.

[tts-break]

Now we are ready for a new question. Once the data is clean, is it arranged in the best shape for analysis?

Sometimes we want many rows and only a few columns. At other times, we want fewer rows and several category columns. The facts may be the same, but the structure is different.

Throughout this module, keep one question in mind. What does one row represent? If you can answer that clearly, pivoting and un pivoting become much easier to understand.

slides.title: Reshaping changes structure
slides.transcript:
Reshaping changes how the information is organized. It should not silently change the meaning of the information.

Long data usually stores categories as values in rows. Wide data usually turns selected category values into separate columns.

[tts-break]

The important caution is that a reshape can also include aggregation. If several source rows are combined into one output cell, we are no longer changing only the layout. We are also reducing detail.

So whenever you reshape data, ask two questions: what structure changed, and did any information get summarized or removed?

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you should be able to recognize long and wide data, explain the grain of each structure, and move between the two forms.

You will learn how to create pivot style results with conditional aggregation, how to un pivot wide columns back into rows, and how to preserve the difference between a missing value and a true zero.

You will also learn how joins and aggregation can change the meaning of a reshape. Most importantly, you should be able to explain why a particular output shape is appropriate for the next analytical task.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript:
We will begin with the basic difference between long and wide data.

Then we will learn how to pivot, which means turning selected row categories into columns. After that, we will reverse the process and un pivot wide columns back into rows.

[tts-break]

Next, we will focus on grain, because grain is the main protection against accidental double counting and information loss.

Finally, we will validate reshaped results and decide whether long or wide form is better for reporting, visualization, or later analysis.

slides.title: Teaching database
slides.transcript:
We will use several small datasets because reshaping appears in many different situations.

Admissions data gives us diagnosis categories. Sales data gives us products, months, and revenue. Survey responses give us question categories. Grades give us student and course combinations.

We also have wide examples such as monthly sales and patient metrics.

The goal is not to memorize one dataset. The goal is to recognize the same reshaping pattern across different kinds of data.

slides.title: Long form
slides.transcript:
Let us begin with long form.

In this example, each row represents one product and one month. The month is stored as a value in a column.

For example, Laptop in January is one row, and Laptop in February is another row.

[tts-break]

This shape is flexible. If April arrives, we usually add another row rather than adding a new column to the table.

Long form works especially well for filtering, grouping, time series analysis, and many visualization tools.

slides.title: Wide form
slides.transcript:
Now compare that with wide form.

Instead of storing January and February as row values, we create separate January and February columns.

The grain has changed. One row now represents one product, while the month information is spread horizontally across columns.

Wide form can be very convenient for scorecards and reports where people want to compare a small number of fixed categories side by side.

slides.title: Same facts, different shape
slides.transcript:
These two tables can represent the same business facts even though they look different.

In long form, Laptop January and Laptop February are two rows. In wide form, those two values appear on one Laptop row under separate month columns.

[tts-break]

This is why reshaping is not simply a visual change. The row meaning changes.

Before you reshape, say the grain out loud. For example: one row per product and month before the reshape, and one row per product after the reshape.

That simple habit makes the rest of the query much easier to reason about.

slides.title: What grain means
slides.transcript:
Grain means the meaning of one row.

A transaction table may have one row per sale. After grouping, the grain may become one row per product per month. After pivoting months into columns, the grain may become one row per product.

If you cannot clearly say what one row represents, it is very difficult to know whether your result is correct.

slides.title: State the grain before writing S Q L
slides.transcript:
Before you write any pivot query, complete one sentence: one output row represents what?

Once that is clear, decide which categories should become columns. Then decide which value or measure should fill those columns.

[tts-break]

Finally, ask whether more than one source row can contribute to the same output cell.

If the answer is yes, you need an aggregation rule such as sum, count, maximum, or average.

slides.title: When long form works well
slides.transcript:
Long form is usually a good choice when categories change over time.

If a new month, product, diagnosis, or survey question appears, it can simply become another row value.

Long form is also natural for filtering, grouping, plotting trends, and many modeling workflows.

A major advantage is that the table structure does not have to change every time a new category appears.

slides.title: When wide form works well
slides.transcript:
Wide form is useful when the categories are stable and the main goal is side by side comparison.

For example, a report may always show January, February, and March in separate columns. A grade matrix may always show a small fixed list of courses.

Wide form is easy for people to scan, but it becomes harder to maintain when categories change frequently.

slides.title: Reshaping can also aggregate
slides.transcript:
A pivot often does more than change layout.

Suppose several sales transactions belong to the same product and month. If we want only one product and month value in the pivot, those transactions must be combined.

[tts-break]

That means we need an aggregation rule. For revenue, we usually add the values together.

At that point, the transformation is doing two things: reshaping the data and reducing transaction level detail.

That is why the aggregation decision must be explicit.

slides.title: Inspect the long admissions data
slides.transcript:
Before pivoting admissions, inspect the source rows first.

Each row represents one admission. Diagnosis is stored as a value in the diagnosis column.

Later, the pivot will create separate diagnosis columns. That query is much easier to understand after you understand the long source.

Always inspect the source grain before you reshape it.

slides.title: A simple pivot mental model
slides.transcript:
A pivot becomes much easier if you break it into four decisions.

First, define the output grain. Second, identify which category values should become columns. Third, choose the measure. Fourth, choose the aggregate used to fill each cell.

For the admissions example, one output row might represent one month. The categories are diagnoses, and the measure is the number of admissions.

slides.title: Conditional aggregation
slides.transcript:
In Postgres, we do not need a special pivot keyword for the patterns in this module.

Instead, we can use conditional aggregation.

One common method uses a case expression inside an aggregate. Postgres also provides the filter clause, which often makes conditional counts and sums easier to read.

Both methods follow the same idea: group the rows, then calculate a separate aggregate for each category we want to display as a column.

slides.title: Pivot with a case expression
slides.transcript:
In the case expression version, the query groups admissions by month.

For each diagnosis column, the case expression checks whether the current row belongs to that diagnosis.

If it matches, the row contributes a value. If it does not match, it contributes zero or nothing, depending on the expression.

The aggregate then combines those contributions into the final monthly count.

slides.title: How to read the case expression pivot
slides.transcript:
When reading a pivot query, separate the grouping logic from the category logic.

The group by part determines the output rows. In this example, it creates one row per month.

The case expression decides which rows contribute to each diagnosis column.

[tts-break]

This is the core pivot pattern: one grouped row, with several category specific aggregate columns.

slides.title: Pivot with the filter clause
slides.transcript:
Postgres also lets us attach a condition directly to an aggregate by using the filter clause.

For example, we can count all rows where diagnosis is Pneumonia, then create another filtered count for Fracture.

This can be easier to read because the aggregate and the condition stay together.

Compare the two versions. The wording is different, but the business meaning is the same.

slides.title: Case expression compared with filter
slides.transcript:
Case expressions and filter are two ways to perform conditional aggregation.

The case expression is flexible and works in many database systems. The filter clause is especially easy to read in Postgres when we create category specific counts or sums.

The more important issue is not which syntax looks better. The important issue is whether the output grain, category conditions, and aggregation rule are correct.

slides.title: Pivot revenue
slides.transcript:
A pivot is not limited to counts.

We can also pivot a measure such as revenue.

For example, one output row can represent one month, while separate columns show Laptop revenue, Mouse revenue, and Keyboard revenue.

In that case, the measure is revenue, and we add the revenue values together for each category.

Always identify both the row grain and the measure before interpreting a pivot result.

slides.title: Pivot survey responses
slides.transcript:
Survey data is another common long form example.

Suppose each row contains one respondent, one question, and one score. We may want one output row per respondent, with question one, question two, and question three as separate columns.

If there is at most one score for each respondent and question combination, an aggregate such as maximum can place that single value into the correct column.

The important assumption is uniqueness. If multiple answers exist for the same respondent and question, you need to decide how those multiple values should be handled.

slides.title: Missing and zero are different
slides.transcript:
A missing pivot cell should not automatically be changed to zero.

Zero can mean that the observation exists and its measured value is zero. A null value can mean that there was no recorded observation at all.

[tts-break]

For example, zero monthly sales may mean we know the product had no sales. A null value may mean we have no record for that product and month.

Those are different facts, and later averages or models may treat them differently.

slides.title: Missing value semantics
slides.transcript:
This example compares two ways to handle a missing category.

If we preserve the null value, a missing response stays missing. If the query forces zero, the result now claims that the value is zero.

That may be correct in some situations, but it should be a business decision, not a convenience decision.

Before replacing a missing value with zero, ask what the missing source row actually means.

slides.title: Validate pivot totals
slides.transcript:
After creating a pivot, validate it.

For additive measures such as revenue, calculate the total from the original source and compare it with the total represented by the pivot.

If they should represent the same observations, the totals should agree.

This simple check can catch missing categories, duplicated rows, and incorrect grouping.

slides.title: Inspect a wide source
slides.transcript:
Now let us reverse the direction.

The monthly sales table is already wide. January, February, and March are separate columns.

That may be convenient for a report, but it can be awkward for filtering, grouping by month, or building a trend chart.

Un pivoting converts those repeated month columns back into row values.

slides.title: The un pivot mental model
slides.transcript:
Un pivoting turns repeated measure columns into rows.

The wide source may have one row per product with several month columns.

The long result will have a month column and a revenue column. One product row can expand into several product and month rows.

So the grain changes from one row per product to one row per product and month.

slides.title: Method one, union all
slides.transcript:
One simple way to un pivot data is to use union all.

We write one select statement for January, another for February, and another for March. Each select returns the same column structure.

Then union all stacks those rows together.

This approach is repetitive, but it is easy to understand because each source column is handled explicitly.

slides.title: Un pivot with union all
slides.transcript:
In the union all query, each select assigns a month label and reads the matching wide revenue column.

After stacking the selects, one product row becomes several rows.

For example, one Laptop row can become Laptop in January, Laptop in February, and Laptop in March.

That is the basic wide to long transformation.

slides.title: Method two, lateral values
slides.transcript:
Postgres also gives us a shorter option called lateral values.

Instead of writing several full select statements, we can create several month and value pairs for each source row.

The lateral part lets those generated pairs use values from the current source row.

This is useful when many wide columns follow the same repeated pattern.

slides.title: Un pivot with lateral values
slides.transcript:
In this pattern, the source table appears once.

For every source row, the values block generates multiple output rows. Each generated row contains a category label, such as a month, and the corresponding value.

The result is long form, just like the union all version.

The difference is mainly in how compactly we express the transformation.

slides.title: Union all compared with lateral values
slides.transcript:
Both methods are useful.

Union all is very explicit and often easier for beginners to read when there are only a few columns.

Lateral values is shorter when many columns follow the same repeated structure.

Choose the method that makes the transformation easiest to understand and maintain.

slides.title: Un pivot patient metrics
slides.transcript:
Patient metrics give us another wide to long example.

Suppose one row contains heart rate, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and oxygen saturation in separate columns.

We can un pivot those columns into two fields: metric name and metric value.

This shape can be useful when we want to apply the same logic across several kinds of measurements.

slides.title: Use one compatible data type
slides.transcript:
When several source columns become one long value column, Postgres needs a compatible data type for those values.

For example, one source column may contain whole numbers while another contains decimal values.

[tts-break]

If the data types do not match, we may need to convert them to one compatible type.

This is important because the long value column must have one consistent type, even though its values came from different source columns.

slides.title: Keep or remove missing cells
slides.transcript:
When un pivoting, decide what to do with missing cells.

One option is to keep them. That preserves the fact that the category exists but the value is missing.

Another option is to remove those generated rows after un pivoting.

Neither choice is automatically correct. The decision depends on whether missingness is meaningful for the analysis.

slides.title: Remove missing values after un pivoting
slides.transcript:
If you decide that missing generated values should not appear in the long result, make that rule explicit.

First un pivot the columns. Then filter out rows where the generated value is null.

This is better than silently losing them because the query clearly documents the decision.

Whenever you remove missing values, explain why they are not needed for the downstream analysis.

slides.title: A pivot and un pivot round trip
slides.transcript:
It is tempting to think that pivoting and then un pivoting will always return the original data.

That is not true.

If the pivot aggregated several transaction rows into one total, the individual transactions have already been lost.

Un pivoting can recover the aggregated product and month totals, but it cannot recreate the original transaction IDs or individual amounts.

slides.title: Round trip example
slides.transcript:
This example makes the round trip idea visible.

The first step creates a wide summary. The second step converts that wide summary back into long form.

The result is long again, but it still contains summarized data.

So a return to long form does not necessarily mean a return to the original detail.

slides.title: Reversible compared with lossy reshaping
slides.transcript:
A reshape is easier to reverse when each source value maps directly to one output value and we keep the category labels.

It becomes lossy when multiple source rows are aggregated into one cell, when categories are combined, or when missing rows are removed.

Always ask what information survives the transformation and what information cannot be recovered afterward.

slides.title: Grain is the safeguard
slides.transcript:
Grain is the main safeguard against incorrect reshaping.

If the source has multiple transactions for Laptop in January, but the wide output has only one Laptop in January cell, then those transaction rows must be combined somehow.

If revenue is the measure, adding the values together may be the correct rule.

But the transaction level detail is no longer present in that cell.

slides.title: Check the source grain
slides.transcript:
Before pivoting, inspect how many source rows exist for each intended output cell.

For example, group the sales by product and month, and then count how many source rows appear in each group.

If some product and month combinations contain more than one transaction, that proves that the pivot requires aggregation.

This type of grain check makes the transformation rule visible before you reshape the data.

slides.title: See what aggregation removes
slides.transcript:
This example compares individual source rows with their aggregated total.

Before aggregation, we can see each transaction separately. After aggregation, we see one combined product and month value.

The total may be perfectly correct, but the individual transaction details cannot be recovered from that total alone.

That is what information loss through aggregation means.

slides.title: Be careful when joining before a pivot
slides.transcript:
Reshaping often happens after joins, and this is where major errors can occur.

A join can create extra row combinations before the pivot even begins.

For example, if one patient has several admissions and several lab results, joining both fact like tables only by patient can create many combinations.

If you aggregate after that join, the pivot may count the same facts more than once and produce totals that are too high.

slides.title: Patient admissions by month
slides.transcript:
Here we join patients to admissions and create monthly admission counts.

The patient table contributes descriptive information. The admissions table contributes the events being counted.

Because we understand the one to many relationship, we can group to one row per patient and create month specific counts.

The join is safe because we know exactly which table contains the facts we are measuring.

slides.title: The risk of one to many multiplication
slides.transcript:
Now consider a more dangerous case.

Suppose one patient has three admissions and four lab results. If we join admissions to lab results only by patient, we can create twelve combined rows.

[tts-break]

If we then count admissions or sum another measure, the results may look reasonable but be wrong because the join multiplied the facts first.

This is why you should check cardinality before reshaping joined data.

slides.title: Summarize before reshaping
slides.transcript:
One way to control row multiplication is to summarize first.

First summarize the fact table to the grain you actually need. Then join or pivot from that stable intermediate result.

This separates the aggregation decision from the presentation decision.

It also makes the query easier to validate because each stage has a clear grain.

slides.title: Summarize sales before the pivot
slides.transcript:
In this example, the first stage creates one row per product, category, and month.

The outer query then pivots those monthly totals into columns.

There are two grain changes, and both are deliberate.

Being able to describe those intermediate grains is one of the best protections against accidental double counting.

slides.title: Categories that change over time
slides.transcript:
Wide pivots work best when the category list is stable.

Suppose the report has January, February, and March columns. When April arrives, the S Q L must be changed if April also needs its own column.

[tts-break]

That tells us something important: the categories are part of the output schema.

If categories change often, keeping the data in long form may be a better design.

slides.title: Discover categories first
slides.transcript:
Before creating a static pivot, inspect the distinct category values in the source.

For example, list all diagnoses or all products.

If new categories are already present but your pivot only has columns for older categories, those new values may disappear from the report.

Checking the categories first helps you decide which columns the report should contain.

slides.title: A static category pivot
slides.transcript:
A static pivot works well when the selected categories are intentionally fixed and are not expected to change often.

For example, a healthcare report may intentionally compare only pneumonia, fracture, and flu.

The benefit is a predictable set of output columns.

The limitation is that a newly appearing diagnosis will not automatically become a new column.

slides.title: Optional cross tab
slides.transcript:
Postgres also offers a cross tab function through an extension.

It can create pivot style results, but it introduces additional setup and requires explicit output column definitions.

For this course, we will mainly use conditional aggregation because the logic is clear and easy to explain.

You can explore cross tab later when you need specialized reporting behavior.

slides.title: Choose the shape for the next task
slides.transcript:
There is no single best data shape.

A wide matrix may be excellent for a fixed dashboard. A long table is often better for trend analysis, flexible filtering, and visualization.

The shape should be chosen based on the next consumer of the data.

Do not reshape just because wide or long looks more familiar.

slides.title: Long form for charting
slides.transcript:
A long monthly product summary is usually convenient for charting.

Each row contains a month, a product, and a measure such as revenue.

A visualization tool can use month on the horizontal axis, revenue as the value, and product as a grouping or color category.

New products and new months can appear as new rows without changing the table structure.

slides.title: Long form compared with wide form
slides.transcript:
Long and wide forms serve different downstream needs.

Long form is usually more flexible for charts, modeling, filtering, and changing categories.

Wide form is often convenient for fixed business reports and side by side comparisons.

A good pipeline can keep a stable long analytical table and create wide presentation outputs only where they are actually needed.

slides.title: Practice one
slides.transcript:
In this practice, the grades table is long.

Each row represents one student and course grade.

Your goal is to create one row per student, with selected course grades in separate columns.

Before writing the query, state the output grain, identify the course categories, and decide how a missing course should appear.

A missing grade should normally remain null rather than being changed to zero.

slides.title: Grade matrix solution
slides.transcript:
The solution groups the data by student and creates one aggregate expression for each course.

The maximum function works here because the exercise assumes at most one grade per student and course combination.

That assumption matters.

If several grades existed for the same student and course, maximum would choose one value and hide the others. So always connect the aggregate choice to the expected grain of the source.

slides.title: Practice two
slides.transcript:
This practice creates a patient by month admission matrix.

The intended output has one row per patient. Month columns contain admission counts, and a total column shows the overall number of admissions.

Because we start from the patient table and use a left join, patients with no admissions can still appear in the result.

Again, state the grain before writing the pivot expressions.

slides.title: Patient and month solution
slides.transcript:
The solution creates separate counts for January, February, and March and also calculates total admissions.

After running it, compare the month specific counts with the total.

If the dataset only contains those months, their sum should agree with the total.

This gives us a built in validation check for the pivot.

slides.title: Retail project
slides.transcript:
The retail project asks you to create two outputs from the same sales facts.

One output stays long and supports trend analysis. The other becomes wide and supports a scorecard style report.

The important idea is that both outputs should represent the same underlying revenue.

The project is not complete until the source total and both transformed totals have been compared.

slides.title: Project validation
slides.transcript:
A strong reshaping project includes validation at every stage.

State the grain before and after the reshape. Compare totals for additive measures. Check whether null values were preserved or intentionally changed. Confirm that expected categories are present.

[tts-break]

Also check joins. Did the row count increase more than expected? Did one to many relationships create duplicated facts?

Validation gives you evidence that the result is actually correct.

slides.title: Recognition checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Use this checkpoint to test whether you understand the ideas, not just the syntax.

Can you explain the row grain? Can you explain why an aggregate is required? Can you explain the difference between missing and zero?

Can you explain why several wide columns need a common data type when they become one long value column?

And can you explain why an aggregated pivot cannot recreate the original transaction rows?

slides.title: Applied challenge
slides.transcript:
The applied challenge asks you to reshape long sales data into one row per product.

Create separate January, February, and March revenue columns.

Preserve null when there is no observation for a product and month unless the business meaning clearly says that missing should be zero.

Before writing the query, state the output grain and the measure that belongs in each pivot cell.

slides.title: Module 10 takeaways
slides.transcript:
The main lesson from Module 10 is not a particular pivot syntax.

The main lesson is to control meaning while changing shape.

State the grain first. Use conditional aggregation for pivots. Use union all or lateral values for un pivoting. Preserve the difference between null and zero. Check joins before aggregating.

And always validate row counts and totals after a reshape.

slides.title: Reshaping decision guide
slides.transcript:
Use a simple decision process.

If category values need to become columns, use a pivot pattern. If repeated columns need to become rows, use an un pivot pattern.

If categories change frequently, long form is usually more flexible. If categories are stable and the output is a fixed matrix, wide form may be appropriate.

And whenever multiple source rows map to one output cell, make the aggregation rule explicit.

slides.title: Next, Module 11
slides.transcript:
In Module 11, we will build on everything you have learned so far and move into more advanced S Q L patterns.

You will work with common table expressions, recursive queries, ranking, lag and lead, running totals, moving averages, and other window function techniques.

[tts-break]

The grain habit from this module will remain important. Advanced S Q L becomes much easier to understand when you can explain what one row represents at every stage of the query.
